headings.title: Introduction to Cancer Care and Treatment Goals
headings.content: Cancer care in nursing encompasses a comprehensive approach aimed at addressing the complex physical, psychological, and emotional needs of individuals diagnosed with malignancies. As nursing students in Nigeria, understanding the foundational goals of cancer treatment is crucial for delivering holistic patient-centered care. Treatment goals generally fall into three primary categories: curative, control, and palliative. Curative therapy intends to eradicate the cancer entirely, offering the patient a disease-free survival period. Control therapy focuses on halting the progression of the disease, preventing further metastasis, and prolonging life when a cure is unattainable. Palliative therapy, on the other hand, prioritizes comfort and the enhancement of quality of life by managing debilitating symptoms, regardless of the stage of the disease. Nurses play an indispensable role in assessing patient responses, educating families, and coordinating interprofessional care teams to align treatments with the patient's personal goals and values. Furthermore, cultural context and resource availability in Nigerian healthcare settings necessitate that nurses are adept at advocating for accessible treatment options while providing compassionate, culturally sensitive support throughout the continuum of care, from initial diagnosis to survivorship or end-of-life care.

headings.title: Surgical Management in Oncology
headings.content: Surgical oncology remains one of the oldest and most effective modalities for the treatment and management of solid tumors. Surgery can be utilized for various purposes, including diagnosis, staging, primary treatment, palliation, and rehabilitation. Diagnostic surgery involves obtaining a tissue biopsy to confirm the histological type of cancer. Staging surgery, such as lymph node dissection, assesses the extent of disease spread. Curative or primary treatment surgery aims to completely remove the localized tumor along with a margin of healthy tissue to ensure clear margins. Palliative surgery is performed not to cure, but to alleviate distressing symptoms such as bowel obstruction, hemorrhage, or severe pain caused by tumor compression. As a nursing student, it is vital to understand the unique perioperative needs of oncology patients, who may be immunocompromised, malnourished, or experiencing organ dysfunction. Preoperative care involves comprehensive assessment, patient education, and psychological support to alleviate anxiety. Postoperative nursing care focuses on monitoring for complications such as hemorrhage, infection, wound dehiscence, venous thromboembolism, and managing pain effectively. Nurses must also facilitate early ambulation, nutritional support, and emotional coping strategies, keeping in mind the patient's long-term body image and functional recovery in the context of Nigerian surgical wards.

headings.title: Principles and Nursing Care of Patients Undergoing Radiation Therapy
headings.content: Radiation therapy utilizes high-energy ionizing radiation to damage the DNA of cancer cells, leading to cellular death while sparing surrounding normal tissues as much as possible. It can be administered externally via teletherapy or internally via brachytherapy, where radioactive sources are placed directly into or near the tumor site. Radiation is used for curative, adjuvant, neo-adjuvant, or palliative purposes. Nursing care for patients undergoing radiation therapy requires rigorous safety protocols, especially when managing sealed or unsealed radioactive sources in brachytherapy, where principles of time, distance, and shielding must be strictly maintained to protect healthcare workers and visitors. For patients receiving external beam radiation, nursing care centers on skin and mucosal management. The skin in the treatment field is fragile; nurses must educate patients to keep the area clean, dry, and free from friction, harsh soaps, lotions, or direct sunlight. Side effects often depend on the anatomical site irradiated and can include localized erythema, desquamation, fatigue, mucositis, xerostomia, and bone marrow suppression. Nurses play a crucial role in nutritional support, psychological encouragement, and monitoring for acute and late radiation toxicities, ensuring patients in resource-constrained Nigerian facilities receive optimal supportive care during their treatment cycles.

headings.title: Chemotherapy Administration and Safety Precautions
headings.content: Chemotherapy involves the use of cytotoxic medications to systemic destroy rapidly dividing cancer cells. Because these drugs affect normal fast-dividing cells (such as bone marrow, hair follicles, and the gastrointestinal tract), they produce significant side effects, including myelosuppression, alopecia, nausea, vomiting, and mucositis. Safe administration of chemotherapy is a critical competency for nursing students. Due to the hazardous nature of antineoplastic agents, strict safety precautions must be observed during preparation, administration, and disposal. Nurses must wear personal protective equipment (PPE), including powder-free chemotherapy gloves, gowns made of low-permeability fabric, and eye protection or respiratory masks when handling drugs or excreta. Chemotherapy should be prepared in certified biological safety cabinets (BSCs) if available. During administration, nurses must monitor closely for extravasation—the inadvertent leakage of vesicant drugs into surrounding subcutaneous tissue—which can cause severe tissue necrosis. Prompt recognition of a burning sensation, swelling, or lack of blood return requires immediate cessation of the infusion and adherence to institutional extravasation protocols. Furthermore, patient education regarding infection prevention (due to neutropenia), bleeding precautions (due to thrombocytopenia), and nutritional maintenance is vital for safe outpatient and inpatient oncology nursing practice in Nigeria.

headings.title: Targeted Therapy and Immunotherapy
headings.content: Targeted therapy and immunotherapy represent modern advancements in oncology that move beyond the generalized cytotoxicity of traditional chemotherapy. Targeted therapy drugs are specifically engineered to interfere with molecular targets—such as specific proteins, enzymes, or receptor sites—that are necessary for the growth, division, and survival of cancer cells, thereby minimizing damage to normal host tissues. Examples include monoclonal antibodies and tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Immunotherapy, conversely, works by harnessing and enhancing the patient's own immune system to recognize and destroy cancer cells. This includes immune checkpoint inhibitors, CAR T-cell therapy, and cancer vaccines. While these therapies offer improved specificity and often fewer systemic side effects than conventional chemotherapy, they introduce unique adverse effect profiles that nurses must monitor closely. Targeted therapies can cause dermatologic toxicities, hypertension, and diarrhea. Immunotherapy frequently triggers immune-related adverse events (irAEs) due to hyperactivation of the immune system, leading to inflammation in organs such as the colon (colitis), lungs (pneumonitis), liver (hepatitis), and endocrine glands (endocrinopathies). As student nurses, understanding the mechanisms of action and recognizing early signs of irAEs is essential for timely intervention, patient education, and advocacy, particularly as these newer therapies become more prevalent in comprehensive cancer care centers across Nigeria.

headings.title: Oncological Emergencies and Acute Complications
headings.content: Oncological emergencies are acute, life-threatening complications that can arise as a direct result of the cancer itself or as a side effect of oncological treatments. Prompt recognition and rapid nursing intervention are critical for survival. Common oncological emergencies include superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO), spinal cord compression, tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), hypercalcemia of malignancy, and severe neutropenic sepsis. Spinal cord compression occurs when a tumor invades the epidural space, presenting with progressive back pain, motor weakness, sensory loss, and bowel or bladder dysfunction, requiring urgent corticosteroid therapy and radiation or surgery. Tumor lysis syndrome happens rapidly when massive numbers of cancer cells are destroyed simultaneously, releasing intracellular contents into the bloodstream and causing hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia, which can lead to acute kidney injury and cardiac arrhythmias. Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency characterized by fever in a patient with a severely low neutrophil count, requiring immediate blood cultures and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within the golden hour. As Nigerian nurses, remaining vigilant, conducting baseline risk assessments, and understanding emergency escalation pathways can mean the difference between life and death for vulnerable oncology patients experiencing acute complications.

headings.title: Pain and Symptom Management in Cancer
headings.content: Pain and symptom management are central pillars of quality oncological nursing care. Cancer pain can be somatic, visceral, or neuropathic, arising from tumor invasion, nerve compression, or treatment side effects. Effective pain management relies on comprehensive, regular assessment using validated pain scales, adhering to the WHO analgesic ladder, and utilizing a multimodal approach that combines pharmacological agents (non-opioids, weak opioids, and strong opioids like morphine) with non-pharmacological interventions such as positioning, massage, heat/cold therapy, and psychological support. Nurses must dispel myths regarding opioid addiction when treating cancer pain, ensuring patients receive adequate dosing around the clock with breakthrough medication available. Beyond pain, patients frequently suffer from cancer-related fatigue, nausea, vomiting, cachexia, constipation, and dyspnea. Antiemetics should be administered proactively for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV). Nutritional counseling and appetite stimulants assist in managing wasting syndromes. In resource-constrained settings in Nigeria, where access to specialized palliative medications can sometimes be challenging, nurses must advocate for essential pain management supplies, educate patients and caregivers on proper medication administration, and provide continuous compassionate support to alleviate the profound physical burden of advanced cancer.

headings.title: Psychosocial Support and Palliative Care
headings.content: Psychosocial support and palliative care address the holistic well-being of cancer patients and their families, acknowledging that a cancer diagnosis impacts emotional, social, spiritual, and physical domains. Anxiety, depression, fear of recurrence, and existential distress are common emotional responses throughout the cancer trajectory. Nurses act as therapeutic communicators, providing a safe space for patients to express their fears, grief, and spiritual concerns. Palliative care is not limited to end-of-life care; rather, it should be integrated early alongside active disease-modifying treatments to optimize quality of life from the time of diagnosis. It involves interprofessional collaboration—including social workers, chaplains, physicians, and nurses—to address complex symptom burdens, family coping dynamics, advance care planning, and grief support. In the Nigerian cultural context, where extended families play a significant role in healthcare decision-making and discussions surrounding terminal illness can carry heavy social stigmas, nurses must skillfully bridge communication between patients and their families. Providing culturally congruent end-of-life care ensures dignity, pain relief, and emotional closure, making the nurse an essential advocate for both the patient and their grieving family members.
